longest-common-subsequence.pattern: Two-string DP: dp[i][j] over prefixes (match → diagonal + 1, else max of dropping one)

approaches.name: Recursion on the first characters
approaches.idea: Compare the first characters: if they match, they can both be part of the subsequence; if not, the answer drops one of them.
steps: `lcs(i, j)`: 0 if either string is used up.
approaches.why: Mismatches branch in two, and the same `(i, j)` pairs are reached many times.

approaches.name: 2-D table over prefixes
approaches.idea: `dp[i][j]` = LCS length of the first `i` characters of `a` and the first `j` of `b`. A matching last character extends the diagonal; otherwise drop the last character of one string.
steps: Row 0 and column 0 are 0 (an empty prefix).
approaches.why: Every pair of prefix lengths is computed once in O(1).

approaches.name: Two rows
approaches.idea: Row `i` only reads row `i − 1`, so keep just the previous and the current row (sized by the shorter string).
steps: For each `i`, fill `cur[j]` with the same rule using `prev[j − 1]`, `prev[j]` and `cur[j − 1]`.
Swap the rows; return `prev[n]` at the end.
approaches.why: Same work, two rows of memory (swap the strings so the rows use the shorter one).

approaches.name: Recursion on the first characters
approaches.idea: If the first characters match, keep both and move on. Otherwise one of them must be deleted: try both and take the cheaper.
steps: `cost(i, j)`: if one word is used up, delete everything left in the other.
Otherwise return `1 + min(cost(i + 1, j), cost(i, j + 1))`.
approaches.why: Branches twice on every mismatch with repeated states.

approaches.name: Through the longest common subsequence
approaches.idea: After the deletions both words equal some common subsequence. Keeping the longest one deletes the fewest characters: `m + n − 2·LCS`.
steps: Compute the LCS length with the standard 2-D table.
approaches.why: One LCS table of (m + 1)(n + 1) entries.

approaches.name: Direct deletion DP with one row
approaches.idea: `dp[i][j]` = deletions to make the first `i` and first `j` characters equal: the diagonal when the last characters match, otherwise 1 + the cheaper deletion. Keep one row plus the old diagonal value.
steps: `row[j] = j` (delete all of the second prefix).
For each `i`: remember `diag = row[0]`, set `row[0] = i`; for each `j`, `next = match ? diag : 1 + min(row[j], row[j − 1])`; then `diag = row[j]` (old), `row[j] = next`.
approaches.why: Same table, one row of memory.

longest-palindromic-substring.pattern: Expand around each of the 2n − 1 centres

approaches.name: Check every substring
approaches.idea: Test every substring with two pointers and keep the longest palindrome.
steps: For every `i <= j`, check whether `s[i..j]` is a palindrome by comparing from both ends.
approaches.why: n²/2 substrings, each checked in O(n).

approaches.name: DP table of palindromic substrings
approaches.idea: `pal[i][j]` is true when `s[i] == s[j]` and the inside `s[i + 1..j − 1]` is a palindrome (or has length < 2). Fill it by increasing `i` from the end so the inside is ready first.
steps: For `i` from n − 1 down to 0, for `j` from `i` to n − 1: `pal[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] && (j − i < 2 || pal[i + 1][j − 1])`.
Whenever `pal[i][j]` is true and longer than the best, record it.
approaches.why: n²/2 entries, each O(1); the table itself is n².

approaches.name: Expand around every centre
approaches.idea: Every palindrome is symmetric about a centre: a character (odd length) or the gap between two characters (even length). From each of the 2n − 1 centres, grow outwards while the ends match.
steps: For each `i`, expand from `(i, i)` and from `(i, i + 1)`.
Expanding: while `l >= 0`, `r < n` and `s[l] == s[r]`, move `l` left and `r` right; the palindrome is `s[l + 1..r − 1]`.
approaches.why: Each expansion is O(n) in the worst case (e.g. "aaaa…"), for 2n − 1 centres, with no table. (Manacher's algorithm reaches O(n) by reusing mirrored expansions, but is rarely expected.)

longest-palindromic-subsequence.pattern: Interval DP: lps(i, j) from lps(i + 1, j − 1), lps(i + 1, j), lps(i, j − 1)

approaches.name: Recursion on the two ends
approaches.idea: If the two ends match, they wrap a palindrome around the best answer for the inside. Otherwise drop one end.
approaches.why: Mismatches branch in two and overlapping ranges are recomputed.

approaches.name: 2-D interval table
approaches.idea: Fill `dp[i][j]` for every range, from short ranges to long ones (by starting `i` at the end), so the inner ranges are ready.
steps: For `i` from n − 1 down to 0, for `j` from `i + 1` to n − 1: `dp[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] ? dp[i + 1][j − 1] + 2 : max(dp[i + 1][j], dp[i][j − 1])`.
approaches.why: About n²/2 ranges, O(1) each.

approaches.name: One row (row i + 1 rolled into row i)
approaches.idea: Row `i` only reads row `i + 1`. Keep one array holding row `i + 1`; while filling row `i` left to right, save the old value of `dp[j − 1]` (that is `dp[i + 1][j − 1]`) before overwriting it.
steps: For `i` from n − 1 down to 0: `row[i] = 1`; `diag = 0` (dp[i + 1][i]); for `j` from `i + 1`: `old = row[j]`; `row[j] = s[i] == s[j] ? diag + 2 : max(row[j], row[j − 1])`; `diag = old`.
approaches.why: Same work in one row. (Equivalently: the LCS of `s` and its reverse.)

palindromic-substrings.pattern: Expand around each of the 2n − 1 centres, counting as you grow

approaches.name: Check every substring
approaches.idea: Test each of the n(n + 1)/2 substrings with two pointers and count the palindromes.
steps: For every `i <= j`, check `s[i..j]` from both ends.
approaches.why: n²/2 substrings, each checked in O(n).

approaches.name: DP table of palindromic substrings
approaches.idea: `pal[i][j]` is true when the ends match and the inside is a palindrome. Fill it from the end and count the true entries.
steps: For `i` from n − 1 down to 0, `j` from `i` up: `pal[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] && (j − i < 2 || pal[i + 1][j − 1])`.
Count the entries that are true.
approaches.why: n²/2 entries at O(1) each, stored in a table.

approaches.name: Expand around every centre
approaches.idea: From each of the 2n − 1 centres (characters and gaps), grow outwards while the ends match. Every successful step is one more palindromic substring.
steps: For each centre `(i, i)` and `(i, i + 1)`: while `l >= 0`, `r < n` and `s[l] == s[r]`, count one and move outwards.
approaches.why: The total expansion work equals the number of palindromes found plus 2n − 1 failed checks, at most O(n²), with no table.

interleaving-string.pattern: Two-string DP: can the first i of s1 and j of s2 form the first i + j of s3?

approaches.name: Recursion choosing the next source
approaches.idea: The next character of `s3` must come from the front of `s1` or the front of `s2`. Try whichever matches (both, if both do).
steps: If the lengths do not add up, return false.
`can(i, j)`: true when both are used up.
approaches.why: When both fronts match, both branches are explored, and the same `(i, j)` repeats.

approaches.name: 2-D table over prefixes
approaches.idea: `dp[i][j]` = can `s1[0..i)` and `s2[0..j)` interleave into `s3[0..i + j)`? The last character came from `s1` or from `s2`.
steps: If lengths do not add up, return false. `dp[0][0] = true`.
approaches.why: Every pair of prefix lengths once.

approaches.name: One row
approaches.idea: Row `i` only needs row `i − 1` (same column) and the current row (column to the left), so one boolean array is enough.
steps: `row[0] = true` initially; for each `i` from 0 to m, for each `j` from 0 to n, update `row[j]` in place.
`row[j]` (still holding row `i − 1`) stays true only if `s1[i − 1]` matches; OR it with `row[j − 1] && s2[j − 1]` matching.
approaches.why: Same work with n + 1 booleans.

edit-distance.pattern: Two-string DP: insert, delete or replace from the three neighbouring cells

approaches.name: Recursion on the first characters
approaches.idea: If the first characters match, no edit is needed for them. Otherwise one edit happens here: insert, delete or replace; try all three.
steps: `dist(i, j)`: if `word1` is used up, insert the rest of `word2`; if `word2` is used up, delete the rest of `word1`.
Otherwise `1 + min(dist(i, j + 1) /* insert */, dist(i + 1, j) /* delete */, dist(i + 1, j + 1) /* replace */)`.
approaches.why: Three branches on every mismatch with massive repetition.

approaches.name: 2-D table over prefixes
approaches.idea: `dp[i][j]` = edits to turn the first `i` characters of `word1` into the first `j` of `word2`. Matching last characters cost nothing; otherwise take 1 + the cheapest of the three neighbouring cells.
approaches.why: Every pair of prefixes once.

approaches.name: One row plus the saved diagonal
approaches.idea: Keep row `i − 1` in an array and update it to row `i` in place, saving the old left-diagonal value in a variable before it is overwritten.
steps: For each `i`: `diag = row[0]`, `row[0] = i`; for each `j`: `old = row[j]`; `row[j] = match ? diag : 1 + min(diag, row[j], row[j − 1])`; `diag = old`.
approaches.why: Same work, one row of n + 1 integers.

distinct-subsequences.pattern: Two-string counting DP: use s[i] for t[j] (if equal) or skip s[i]

approaches.name: Recursion: use or skip each character of s
approaches.idea: Walk through `s`. Each character can be skipped; if it equals the next needed character of `t`, it can also be used to match it.
approaches.why: Two branches per character of `s` with overlapping states.

approaches.name: 2-D table over prefixes
approaches.idea: `dp[i][j]` = ways the first `i` characters of `s` contain the first `j` of `t` as a subsequence. Either `s[i − 1]` is not used (`dp[i − 1][j]`), or it matches `t[j − 1]` and is used (`dp[i − 1][j − 1]`).
steps: `dp[i][0] = 1` for every `i` (the empty `t` is matched once).
approaches.why: Every pair of prefixes once. Counts in the middle of the table can exceed 64 bits although the answer fits in 32, so the sums wrap modulo 2³² on purpose (Java `int`, C++ `unsigned`, JS `>>> 0`) — the final value is still exact.

approaches.name: One row, updated from right to left
approaches.idea: Keep `ways[j]` for the prefix of `s` seen so far. For each new character of `s`, update `j` from right to left so `ways[j − 1]` still holds the value from before this character.
steps: For each character `c` of `s`, for `j` from n down to 1: if `c == t[j − 1]`, `ways[j] += ways[j − 1]`.
approaches.why: Same work in one row, with the same deliberate 32-bit wrap-around.

regular-expression-matching.pattern: Two-string DP: a star either matches zero copies (skip it) or one more character

approaches.name: Recursion on the pattern
approaches.idea: Check whether the first characters match. If the next pattern character is `*`, either skip the starred element entirely, or (if the first character matches) use it for one character of `s` and stay on the same pattern position.
steps: `match(i, j)`: if the pattern is used up, the string must be too.
approaches.why: Each star branches in two and the same `(i, j)` repeats.

approaches.name: Memoised recursion on (i, j)
approaches.idea: The result depends only on the positions `(i, j)`, so cache it: (m + 1)(n + 1) states.
steps: Same recursion as the brute force.
approaches.why: Each state is computed once with O(1) work.

approaches.name: Bottom-up table from the ends
approaches.idea: `dp[i][j]` = does `s[i..]` match `p[j..]`? Fill it from the back with the same rules, so no recursion is needed.
steps: For `i` from m down to 0 and `j` from n − 1 down to 0: compute `first`; if `p[j + 1] == "*"`, `dp[i][j] = dp[i][j + 2] || (first && dp[i + 1][j])`; else `dp[i][j] = first && dp[i + 1][j + 1]`.
approaches.why: Each cell once with O(1) work; i goes up to m so an empty rest of `s` against a pattern like `a*b*` is handled.
